title: The Light of the World and Before Abraham, I Am
summary: The chapter opens with the account of a woman caught in adultery, whom Jesus refuses to condemn while telling her to sin no more; this passage is missing from the earliest manuscripts of John. In the temple courts Jesus then declares, “I am the light of the world,” and argues with his opponents about his testimony, his origin, and true freedom. The debate grows fierce over who is a true child of Abraham, and it ends when Jesus says, “before Abraham was born, I am,” and the crowd picks up stones.
story: We are still in Jerusalem during or just after the Feast of Tabernacles, and the arguments of chapter 7 intensify. Chapter 7 asked where Jesus comes from; chapter 8 answers with the boldest claims yet. He is the light of the world, he comes from above, he speaks what the Father taught him, and he existed before Abraham. The chapter also records a sharp breakdown. It begins with people believing in him (8:30-31) and ends with those same hearers trying to stone him, which shows how shallow belief can turn to hostility when Jesus names what it will cost.
historical:
John 7:53-8:11, the story of the woman caught in adultery, is not found in the earliest Greek manuscripts of John, including two papyri copied around AD 200 and the great fourth-century codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. The first surviving Greek manuscript to include it is Codex Bezae, from about the fifth century. Where it appears, it isn't always in the same place: some manuscripts put it after John 7:36, 7:44, or 21:25, and one group places it after Luke 21:38. Several manuscripts mark it with signs of doubt, and the earliest Greek commentators on John pass over it. Its vocabulary and style are closer to Luke's than to John's. On the other side, the story was known early. The church historian Eusebius reports that Papias, in the early second century, told of a woman accused of many sins before the Lord, and a third-century church manual, the Didascalia Apostolorum, alludes to a story like this one. Jerome included it in his Latin translation, and Augustine suggested some had removed it for fear it would seem to excuse adultery. Most textual scholars conclude that the passage was not part of John's original Gospel but preserves an early and likely genuine tradition about Jesus; a minority defend it as original. Most modern Bibles, the BSB among them, print it with a note or in brackets.

The argument that follows is one of the most painful texts in the history of Jewish and Christian relations. In 8:44 Jesus tells his opponents, “You belong to your father, the devil.” The hearers are specific: John says they are “the Jews who had believed Him” (8:31), people within Jesus' own community whose faith turns to violent rejection. The language belongs to the tradition of Israel's own prophets, who used fierce words against their own people. Yet this verse was later lifted out of context and used to brand the Jewish people as a whole children of the devil, a slander repeated in medieval polemic and in Nazi propaganda. Faithful reading has to name that history plainly: the verse addresses a particular group that wanted Jesus dead, not a people, and it gives no Christian any warrant for contempt.
cultural:
The law of Moses prescribed death for adultery, for both the man and the woman (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22). The accusers bring only the woman, which shows the charge was more about trapping Jesus than about justice. The trap had two jaws. If Jesus said to stone her, he would appear harsh and would defy Roman rule, which reserved capital punishment to the governor (18:31); if he said to release her, he could be accused of setting aside Moses. What Jesus wrote on the ground isn't recorded, and guesses have no support in the text.

The treasury (8:20) was in the temple's Court of the Women, where offering chests stood. This was also where, during Tabernacles, great lamps were lit at night so that, the Mishnah says, their light shone over all Jerusalem. Jesus' claim to be the light of the world was spoken in that setting. The debate about Abraham turns on descent. To be a child of Abraham was the heart of Israel's identity and hope, since God's promises were made to him and his offspring (Genesis 12; 15; 17). Jesus argues that true sonship is shown by resembling the father in deeds.
literary: The main discourse (8:12-59) is a running debate, the sharpest in the Gospel, built on a chain of challenges and replies. It turns on the phrase “I am” in Greek, egō eimi. It first appears with a predicate, “I am the light of the world” (8:12), the second of John's seven “I am” sayings with an image. Then it stands alone: “unless you believe that I am He” (8:24), “then you will know that I am He” (8:28), where the BSB supplies He, and finally “before Abraham was born, I am” (8:58). These absolute uses echo God's self-naming to Moses in Exodus 3:14 and the Greek translation of Isaiah 43:10, where God says his people should know that I am. The stones in 8:59 show the hearers understood the claim. The themes of witness, freedom and slavery, fatherhood, and truth and lies weave together throughout.

outline.t: The woman caught in adultery (absent from the earliest manuscripts)
I am the light of the world; the Father testifies
From above: unless you believe that I am He
The truth will set you free
Children of Abraham, children of God, or of the devil
Before Abraham was born, I am

doctrines.note: “Everyone who sins is a slave to sin” (8:34). Sin here is not only a wrong act but a bondage that no descent or religious standing can break. The hearers insist they have never been slaves, and the chapter shows how sin blinds people to their own condition.

Freedom comes from the Son: “if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (8:36). It is received by continuing in his word (8:31), which marks true disciples. In the adultery account, mercy comes first and the call to holiness follows it: “Then neither do I condemn you” and “Now go and sin no more.”

The absolute “I am” sayings identify Jesus with the God who revealed his name to Moses. John presents this as the core of Christian confession: Jesus is not a created being who began to exist, but the one who is before Abraham.

words.note: Eimi, to be. It is one of the most common Greek verbs, but in this chapter Jesus uses its first person, egō eimi (I am), in ways that go far beyond ordinary speech. In 8:58 the contrast is sharp: Abraham came to be, but Jesus simply is. The verb tenses carry the point, since Abraham was born in the past while Jesus speaks of his existence in the present.

Phōs, light. In the Bible light stands for God's presence, truth, and salvation (Psalm 27:1; Isaiah 9:2; 49:6). John's prologue calls the Word the true light coming into the world (1:9). Here Jesus claims it of himself, and chapter 9 will show it in action as he gives sight to a man born blind.

Alētheia, truth. In John truth is more than accurate information. It is the reality of God made known, and Jesus will say that he himself is the truth (14:6). The truth that sets free (8:32) is not an idea but a relationship with the one who speaks it.

Eleutheroō, to set free. The hearers take it politically and ethnically, as if Jesus called them slaves of a foreign master, but Jesus means freedom from sin. The word recalls the exodus, when God freed Israel from slavery.

christ: This chapter contains some of the plainest claims to deity in the Gospels. Jesus is the light of the world that Isaiah promised would reach the nations. He is from above and not of this world. He will be lifted up (8:28), John's double word for crucifixion and exaltation, and in that lifting people will know who he is. He existed before Abraham and speaks the name of God as his own. And he is the one who, whatever the history of the passage, is remembered in the church as refusing to condemn a sinner while calling her to a new life, which is exactly what the rest of the Gospel says he came to do (3:17).

hard.q: Should the story of the woman caught in adultery be in the Bible?
hard.a:
The evidence set out above is strong that the passage was not part of John's Gospel as first written. It is missing from the earliest and most reliable manuscripts, it moves around among the ones that include it, and its style differs from John's. Most evangelical, Catholic, and critical scholars accept this. Yet the story has strong claims to be a genuine memory of Jesus. It was known in the second and third centuries, it fits what the Gospels elsewhere show of Jesus' dealings with sinners and his opponents' traps, and it does not look like a later invention, since its apparent leniency troubled some early readers.

Churches handle it differently. The Roman Catholic Church regards it as canonical Scripture, the Eastern churches read it in their liturgy, and many Christians in every tradition have received it as Scripture for many centuries. Many Protestant scholars treat it as a true account about Jesus that can be preached with a clear note about its textual history, while others think it should not be treated as Scripture in the full sense. Nothing in Christian doctrine depends on this passage alone, and its teaching of mercy with a call to holiness is found throughout the Gospels. The honest course is the one most Bibles now follow: print it, mark it, and explain it.

questions: The accusers leave one by one, oldest first. What does it take to recognize yourself in Jesus' words, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her”?
The hearers insist they have never been slaves. Where might you be bound in ways you are reluctant to admit?
Jesus' strongest words are aimed at people who had believed in him. What does this chapter suggest about the difference between initial belief and continuing in his word?
